best_field_traits: CEREAL RYE is a cultivated/escaped INTRODUCED cool-season cereal grass with long narrow terminal spikes and rows of overlapping spikelets bearing long awns; each spikelet usually has two fertile florets. Contrast with Hordeum pusillum: true barley makes triads of 3 spikelets at rachis nodes. Rye is not a Hays-native restoration grass.
RACHIS: ONE sessile, typically TWO-fertile-flowered spikelet at each alternating node of a two-ranked unbranched terminal spike; do not confuse florets with spikelets.
GLUMES: two narrow awl-like 1-veined bracts, FNA genus 8–20 mm (NZ cultivated treatment 7–12.5 mm), with scabrous/ciliate keel and short awnlet often 1–3 mm.
LEMMAS: firm five-veined, sharply keeled, usually ~14–18 mm in Australian treatment; conspicuously pectinate-ciliate keel and upper margins; long terminal lemma awn ~20–50 mm (other treatments vary).
TRUE COLLAR: short truncate/lacerate membranous ligule (~0.5–1.5 mm in NZ cultivated treatment); small auricles often present, sometimes obscure. Annual/biennial fibrous roots, no creeping rhizomes.

Count ONE spikelet per rye rachis node versus THREE one-flowered spikelets at each barley node; inside rye spikelet count usually TWO fertile florets.
Distinguish short glume awnlets from much longer terminal LEMMA awns; inspect rough comb-ciliate lemma keel.
Inspect true inner collar ligule and small auricles; head shape/awn length alone cannot separate cultivated or escaped cereals.

diagnostic_species_finalization_20261023.look_here_first: CEREAL RYE (INTRODUCED): find a fibrous-rooted cool-season cereal with one narrow unbranched, often awned terminal SPIKE, not a branched oat panicle. Follow the rachis: ONE sessile spikelet alternates at each node, usually containing TWO fertile florets (sometimes a reduced third). Under 10–20× verify two narrow one-veined awl-like glumes, and five-veined sharply keeled lemmas with rough/ciliate keels and long terminal awns. At the true leaf collar check a short MEMBRANOUS ligule and small auricles when present. Hordeum has THREE spikelets per node; wheat has broader multi-flowered spikelets; wildryes have paired spikelets. Not a Hays-native restoration grass.
diagnostic_species_finalization_20261023.growth_form: Cool-season fibrous-rooted annual or occasionally biennial cereal, commonly ~50–150 cm in NZ treatment; no rhizomes.
diagnostic_species_finalization_20261023.spike_and_spikelets: Two-ranked unbranched spike, ~4–30 cm in NZ treatment; ONE sessile spikelet per rachis node, usually TWO fertile florets, sometimes reduced third; FNA genus spikelet 10–18 mm.
diagnostic_species_finalization_20261023.glumes: Two narrow, 1-veined, rough-keeled awl-like glumes: 8–20 mm in FNA genus, 7–12.5 mm in NZ cultivated subsp. cereale; glume awnlets often ~1–3 mm. Source ranges differ.
diagnostic_species_finalization_20261023.fertile_lemma: Five-veined firm, strongly keeled lemma, commonly 14–18 mm in Australian treatment (broader 10–20 mm NZ); comb-like cilia on keel and margins; terminal awn ~20–50 mm in Australian treatment, ~15–65 mm in NZ.
diagnostic_species_finalization_20261023.ligule_and_collar: Short membranous, often truncate/lacerate ligule, ~0.5–1.5 mm NZ; small auricles often present (~0.5–1 mm in FNA genus), but sometimes obscure. Check actual junction.
local_lookalikes: Hordeum pusillum: THREE one-flowered spikelets per rachis node, versus ONE usually two-flowered rye spikelet.
Triticum aestivum: broader multi-flowered spikelets and broader glumes; examine attached node and lemma keel, not head color.
Elymus virginicus: paired multi-flowered spikelets at nodes with different glume bases; do not infer rye from slender awns.
Avena fatua: open branched panicle with hanging spikelets and bent dorsal lemma awns.

field_photo_quickcheck.heading: Rye: flowering ear → measured true ligule/collar → individual mature spikelet
steps: FIRST see Rasbak's source-labelled photo of an attached flowering rye ear: narrow green-blue ear with upward-pointing awns and yellow hanging pollen anthers. This is authentic reproductive architecture, not an isolated spikelet.

NEXT open the TRUE INNER BLADE–SHEATH JUNCTION: Stefan.lefnaer's verified original photo shows a short membranous rye ligule on the inner side with a photographed 3-mm reference; don't call the outer sheath margin the ligule.

LOOK AT COLLAR AND AURICLES: another Stefan.lefnaer panel contains four real rye collar and sheath views with a 10-mm reference. Use them to learn ear-like clasping projections versus the little inner ligule.

FINALLY inspect the two detached Matt Lavin rye spikelet photographs: two comparatively large florets and small paired glumes; their individual insertions are not safely arrow-labelled yet and no same-plant dissection has been recorded.

NEXT PHOTOGRAPH NEEDED: a rooted entire rye plant showing the living fibrous crown and attached flowering stalk in one view, plus a same-scale comparison to little barley, wheat and Canada wildrye (existing separate images are NOT photographed at matched scale).
PUBLIC PHOTO RIGHTS: one older CC BY-NC research photo stays archived but is excluded from the unrestricted public learner.

VISUAL LOOK-ALIKE CHECK: the final two photos show different species Canada wildrye and little barley with their own source/rights metadata. Compare head posture and branch architecture before fine spikelet identification; they are NOT rye anatomy pictures.

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 01 · LOOK HERE FIRST — UNBRANCHED RYE SPIKE
field_id_short_tiles.short: One narrow two-ranked terminal spike, not a loose branched oat panicle.
field_id_short_tiles.details: Follow the central rachis on the attached flowering ear (panel 0): rye bears ONE sessile spikelet at successive alternating rachis nodes, typically with TWO fertile florets and sometimes a reduced third. Source-labelled detached rye spikelets are shown in panels 4–5, but none proves a calibrated attached node. Do not substitute an old CC BY-NC research image for the public-ready ear. Cultivated rye is introduced, not a Hays-native restoration species.
field_id_short_tiles.status: SOURCE-IDENTIFIED PHOTO — ATTACHED NODE STILL NEEDED

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 02 · ROOTED ANNUAL AND ACTUAL COLLAR
field_id_short_tiles.short: Fibrous-rooted cool-season cereal; short 0.5–1.5 mm membranous ligule, sometimes small auricles.
field_id_short_tiles.details: Inspect the actual blade–sheath junction: panel 1 shows multiple rye collar/auricle angles beside a 10-mm reference, and panel 2 shows the true membranous ligule with a photographed 3-mm scale. Published ligule ranges are approximately 0.5–1.5 mm (New Zealand cultivated rye treatment) or 1–2 mm (VicFlora); do not claim a new specimen measurement from the source scale without calibrated pixel review. Auricles may be small or obscure. Neither collar photograph establishes a connected rooted Texas plant.
field_id_short_tiles.status: GENUINE SCALED COLLAR/LIGULE PHOTOS INSTALLED; ROOTED SAME-PLANT VIEW STILL MISSING

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 03 · COUNT SPIKELETS PER RACHIS NODE
field_id_short_tiles.short: Rye = ONE usually two-flowered spikelet per node; barley = THREE one-flowered spikelets.
field_id_short_tiles.details: Examine one intact mature rachis node at 10–20×: rye has ONE usually two-flowered spikelet per node; little barley has THREE one-flowered spikelets. Panel 0 shows an attached flowering rye ear, panels 4–5 show detached rye spikelets, and panel 7 is a correctly labeled DIFFERENT-species little barley comparison. None is a same-scale, fully exposed rye-versus-barley rachis-node dissection. Wheat also has one spikelet per node but generally more florets and broader glumes.
field_id_short_tiles.status: DETACHED SPIKELET PHOTOS — NODE MICRO MISSING

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 04 · GLUMES, LEMMAS AND DIFFERENT AWNS
field_id_short_tiles.short: Two narrow one-veined glumes ~7–12.5 mm in NZ; firm five-veined lemmas ~10–20 mm.
field_id_short_tiles.details: Dissect a mature spikelet and isolate the two stiff rough-keeled glumes (NZ 7–12.5 mm; broader Flora of North America genus 8–20 mm), each with a short glume awnlet. The lemma has a comb-ciliate keel and a much longer terminal awn (NZ 15–65 mm). Do not call the glume awnlet a fertile lemma awn. Existing spikelet panels do not resolve all veins or both awn origins at a calibrated scale.
field_id_short_tiles.status: SOURCE-BASED MEASUREMENTS — DISSECTION WITH SCALE MISSING

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 05 · CENTRAL TEXAS LOOK-ALIKES
field_id_short_tiles.short: Little barley = triple spikelets; wild oat = branched panicle; wheat/wildrye need node dissection.
field_id_short_tiles.details: Gallery panel 6 is Canada wildrye (Elymus canadensis), with paired spikelets; panel 7 is little barley (Hordeum pusillum), with THREE spikelets per rachis node. These are genuine other-species comparisons, not rye anatomical proof. Wild oat (Avena fatua) has a loose branched panicle with bent/twisted dorsal lemma awns. Wheat (Triticum aestivum) often has broader multi-flowered spikelets. Compare actual attached nodes, glumes and floret counts; do not rely on color or awn length alone.

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 06 · PUBLIC-READY GATE AND EXACT HANDOFF
field_id_short_tiles.short: FIELD_READY_PHOTO_GAPS — five archived source photos; new genuine scaled collar

grass_species_finalization_20261026.measured_diagnostic_check: Published: fibrous-rooted annual/biennial; true short membranous ligule ~0.5–1.5 mm and small sometimes-obscure auricles; 2 fertile florets per spikelet; two narrow one-veined glumes ~7–12.5 mm in NZ cultivated treatment (FNA genus 8–20 mm), often with ~1–3 mm glume awnlets; five-veined firm sharply keeled fertile lemma ~10–20 mm, comb-ciliate keel, terminal lemma awn ~15–65 mm (source-dependent). No measured specimen macro proof in current gallery.
